title: Coiled Jade Pig-Dragon (Zhulong)
medium: Carved and polished nephrite jade
creator: Unknown Hongshan jade carver
description: Carved from pale greenish-buff nephrite during the Late Neolithic Hongshan period, this thick slit-ring pendant curls a plump, embryonic serpent body beneath a blunt, wrinkled boar-like snout and pricked ears. Excavated solely from elite cairn burials across the Liao River basin, the zhulong represents one of the earliest ritual prototypes of the Chinese dragon, linking agrarian fertility with celestial metamorphosis.

title: C-Shaped Jade Dragon of Sanxingtala
originLocation: Sanxingtala, Ongniud Banner, Chifeng, Inner Mongolia
medium: Dark olive-green nephrite jade
creator: Unknown Hongshan master lapidary
description: Standing 26 centimeters tall and abraded from a single pebble of dark green nephrite, the Sanxingtala dragon combines an equine or porcine muzzle with a sweeping, wind-blown dorsal mane that curves gracefully above a limbless C-shaped body. Pierced precisely at its center of gravity so it hangs level when suspended on a ritual cord, it bridges Neolithic shamanic jade-working and the classical iconography of the rain-bringing long.

title: Bronze Ritual Tripod Cauldron (Ding) with Taotie Masks
medium: Piece-mold cast bronze
creator: Royal Shang foundry workshop
description: Cast in ceramic piece-molds for royal ancestral sacrifices, the rounded belly of this Shang bronze ding cauldron is dominated by three fierce taotie masks set against fine spiral thunder-patterns (leiwen). Defined by protruding ocular bosses, curled horns, and a split bilateral visage lacking a lower jaw, the taotie served as a liminal guardian mediating offerings between living rulers and ancestral spirits.

title: Protruding-Eyed Bronze Mask (Zongmu) of Cancong
localName: 青銅縱目面具 (Qīngtóng Zòngmù Miànjù)
originLocation: Sacrificial Pit 2, Sanxingdui, Guanghan, Sichuan, China
medium: Cast bronze with traces of pigment
creator: Ancient Shu royal bronze workshop
description: Measuring 1.38 meters across its sweeping beast-like ears, this monumental bronze mask from Sanxingdui Pit 2 projects twin cylindrical pupils 16 centimeters outward from hollow sockets. Scholars link its superhuman anatomy to later chronicles of Cancong, the semi-divine silkworm-king of Shu described as possessing 'vertical protruding eyes' capable of perceiving cosmic realms.

title: Bronze Sacred Tree No. 1 with Dragon and Nine Sun-Birds
originLocation: Sacrificial Pit 2, Sanxingdui, Guanghan, Sichuan, China
medium: Multi-section cast bronze
creator: Ancient Shu royal bronze workshop
anatomy: nine crested solar birds perched on blossoms
sinuous horned dragon descending the trunk
description: Rising nearly four meters high on a three-lobed mountain base, this cast-bronze axis mundi materializes the ancient myth of the Fusang and Ruomu world-trees where nine solar birds rest upon three tiers of fruiting branches. Along the main trunk coils a slender, clawed dragon descending headfirst from heaven, uniting avian solar deities and draconic sky-messengers in a single ritual monument.

title: Bronze Antlered Crane from the Tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng
localName: 曾侯乙青銅鹿角立鶴 (Lùjiǎo Lìhè)
medium: Cast bronze with gold and turquoise inlay
creator: Court foundry of Marquis Yi of Zeng
anatomy: long arched crane neck and spear-like bill
description: Inscribed along its beak with a dedication for Marquis Yi of Zeng, this 1.4-meter bronze sculpture fuses two emblems of immortality—the sky-faring crane and the antler-shedding stag—into an auspicious psychopomp placed beside the ruler's inner coffin. Its outstretched wings and branched antlers are further incised with curling dragons and turquoise accents to guide the deceased spirit skyward.

title: Two-Headed Lacquered Tomb Guardian Beast (Zhenmushou)
medium: Carved wood, natural deer antlers, and black-and-vermilion lacquer
creator: Unknown Chu lacquer-workshop artisan
description: Characteristic of Chu aristocratic burials in the middle Yangtze valley, this eerie wooden guardian rises in two back-to-back serpentine necks crowned with real stag antlers and painted in scrolling vermilion and black lacquer. With glaring eyes and grotesque protruding tongues hanging to its chest, the zhenmushou warded off subterranean malevolence and pacified restless spirits of the earth.

title: Gold Recumbent Stag Plaque with Turquoise Inlays
originLocation: Kurgan 4, Eleke Sazy, Tarbagatai Mountains, Kazakhstan
medium: Repoussé sheet gold inlaid with turquoise and lapis lazuli
creator: Unknown Saka goldsmith
repository: East Kazakhstan Regional Museum of Local History, Oskemen
anatomy: wave-scroll solar antlers along the spine
description: Unearthed from an early Saka royal barrow in the Tarbagatai range of eastern Kazakhstan, this gold plaque renders the sacred steppe stag with legs folded beneath its belly as if hurtling across the heavens. Turquoise and lapis lazuli inlays accentuate the creature's eye, ear, and haunch, embodying the solar swiftness and ancestral protection prized across Eurasian nomadic 'Animal Style' art.

title: Carved Wooden Horned Griffin from Tuekta Kurgan
originLocation: Tuekta Kurgan 1, Altai Mountains, Siberia, Russia
medium: Carved wood and leather (preserved in kurgan permafrost)
creator: Unknown Altai nomadic woodcarver
description: Preserved for over two millennia in the frozen burial lens of Tuekta Kurgan 1 in the high Altai, this sculpted wooden harness finial depicts a fierce eagle-griffin with a deeply curved raptor beak and notched comb. Originally fitted with leather wings and covered in gold foil, such predatory hybrids guarded the horses sacrificed to carry nomadic chieftains into the afterlife.

title: Golden Pectoral from Tovsta Mohyla (Griffins Attacking Horses)
originLocation: Tovsta Mohyla Kurgan, near Pokrov, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Ukraine
medium: Cast, chased, granulated, and filigree 24-karat gold with enamel
creator: Greco-Scythian master goldsmith of the Bosporan workshops
repository: Treasury of the National Museum of the History of Ukraine, Kyiv
description: Excavated by Borys Mozolevsky in 1971 from a royal Scythian burial mound, this crescentic gold collar divides the cosmos into three tiers, culminating in a dramatic lower register where pairs of winged eagle-griffins sink beaks and claws into rearing steppe horses. Rendered in miniature three-dimensional sculpture, the predation scene encodes Scythian solar-chthonic cosmology and the perpetual struggle between supernatural chaos and pastoral order.

title: Ceremonial Antlered Stag-and-Tiger Horse Mask
originLocation: Pazyryk Kurgan 1, Altai Mountains, Siberia, Russia
medium: Felt, leather, dyed blue fur, and sheet gold foil
creator: Unknown Pazyryk nomadic artisan
anatomy: pouncing blue-fur tiger with gold discs
description: Fitted over the head of a sacrificed stallion in the frozen chamber of Pazyryk Kurgan 1, this leather-and-felt mask transforms an earthly mount into a mythical antlered beast attacked along the bridge of its nose by a blue-dyed, gold-spangled tiger. By ritually converting horses into horned celestial stags, Pazyryk funerary regalia equipped the deceased chieftain's cortege to traverse upper and lower worlds.

title: The Pazyryk Knotted-Pile Carpet with Eagle-Griffin Borders
originLocation: Pazyryk Kurgan 5, Altai Mountains, Siberia, Russia
medium: Symmetrically knotted wool pile textile
creator: Unknown Central Asian or West Asian master weaver
description: Preserved in solid ice inside Pazyryk Kurgan 5, the world's oldest surviving knotted-pile carpet frames its central star-rosette field with concentric friezes of grazing fallow stags, mounted steppe horsemen, and square medallions of winged eagle-griffins. Each griffin turns its crested bird-of-prey head sharply backward with raised wings, illustrating the prestige of Achaemenid and Central Asian monster motifs among high-Altai nomadic elites.

title: Earthenware Roof-Tile End (Wadang) of the Azure Dragon
medium: Molded gray earthenware
creator: Imperial Chang'an kiln workshop
anatomy: wide-flung striding limbs with three claws
description: Molded in crisp high relief within a circular eaves-tile medallion, the Azure Dragon twists its lithe, S-curved body dynamically around a central hemispherical boss while striding across the heavens. Placed on the eastern eaves of Western Han ritual and palatial halls in Chang'an, Qinglong governed the vernal constellations of the East and harmonized imperial architecture with the cosmic Five Phases.

title: Roof-Tile End (Wadang) with White Tiger and Vermilion Bird
medium: Molded gray earthenware
creator: Western Han architectural kiln
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
anatomy: roaring feline jaws and arched tiger spine
description: This Western Han ceramic eaves-tile end belongs to the celebrated Si Shen ('Four Directional Deities') architectural series, pairing fierce directional guardians within circular relief frames to ward off evil spirits from palace roofs. Combining muscular feline stride and sweeping avian plumage, the directional beasts anchored the western autumn and southern summer quadrants of Han correlative cosmology.

title: Molded Hollow Tomb Tile of the Four Symbols (Si Xiang)
localName: 漢五方四神畫像磚 (Sì Xiàng)
medium: Stamped and molded gray funerary terracotta
creator: Unknown Han funerary brickmaker
anatomy: directional dragon and tiger flanking cosmic registers
description: Impressed with intricate dies into wet clay before firing, this monumental hollow tomb brick arranges hunting and celestial scenes around the emblematic guardians of the Five Quarters—East, West, South, North, and Sacred Center. Within subterranean Han tomb chambers, such relief bricks transformed the burial vault into a microcosm of the starry firmament protected by the Four Symbols.

title: Monumental Stone Bixie at the Spirit Road of Xiao Jing
localName: 蕭景墓石刻辟邪 (Náncháo Shíkè Bìxié)
medium: Carved limestone
creator: Imperial Liang stone-carving workshop
repository: In situ, Spirit Path of Marquis Xiao Jing, Nanjing
anatomy: gaping roaring jaws with protruding tongue
description: Guarding the sacred avenue (shendao) of Xiao Jing, cousin to Emperor Wu of Liang, for fifteen centuries, this monolithic limestone chimera arches its back and thrusts out a colossal chest in a display of coiled supernatural power. Widely celebrated today as the civic emblem of Nanjing, Southern Dynasties stone bixie represent the sculptural zenith of early medieval Chinese monumental guardian beasts.

title: Earthenware Human-Faced Tomb Guardian Spirit (Zhenmushou)
medium: Molded earthenware with polychrome and glaze
creator: Unknown Tang funerary ceramicist
anatomy: stern human visage with flaring brows
tall twisted single horn or flame-spike
cloven ungulate hooves on rockwork plinth
description: Seated upright on its haunches atop a craggy pedestal, this Tang funerary guardian merges a furrowed human face with a towering horn, elephantine ears, flaming shoulder-wings, and cloven hooves. Paired at tomb entrances alongside a lion-faced counterpart and armored Lokapalas, the apotropaic hybrid identified as 'Tubo' or 'Qitou' repelled corpse-devouring demons during funerary rites.

title: Sancai-Glazed Lion-Faced Tomb Guardian Beast (Zhenmushou)
localName: 唐三彩獸面鎮墓獸 (Sāncǎi Zhènmùshòu)
medium: Earthenware with three-color (sancai) lead-silicate glaze
creator: Unknown Tang metropolitan kiln master
repository: National Museum of Asian Art (Freer and Sackler Galleries), Washington, D.C.
anatomy: amber, green, and cream sancai glaze drips
description: Drenched in mottled amber, emerald-green, and cream lead glazes, this eighth-century Tang guardian beast bares feline fangs beneath sweeping horns and serrated wing-flames rising from its shoulders. Placed at the threshold of aristocratic subterranean tombs, its ferocious composite form harnessed demonic ferocity to protect the deceased official's soul.

title: Nine Dragons (Jiulong Tu) Handscroll — Detail of Dragon in Clouds
medium: Ink and touches of cinnabar red on paper handscroll
creator: Chen Rong (陳容, active c. 1235–1262)
anatomy: branching stag-like horns and whiskered snout
serpentine scaled body vanishing into mist
flaming dorsal spines and streaming mane
description: Painted in 1244 by the Southern Song scholar-official Chen Rong—renowned for splashing ink while intoxicated and smearing storm-clouds with his cap—Nine Dragons is the supreme masterwork of Chinese dragon painting. Emerging from roiling whirlpools, craggy precipices, and ink-washed thunderheads, its nine dragons embody Daoist cosmic yang energy and ceaseless elemental transformation.

title: Silk Kesi Tapestry with Fenghuang (Chinese Phoenix) and Deer
medium: Slit-tapestry woven silk (kesi)
creator: Unknown Yuan imperial silk-weaving workshop
description: Woven in the painstaking slit-tapestry technique known as kesi ('cut silk'), this Yuan dynasty textile pairs a soaring fenghuang with spotted deer, blossoms, and butterflies across luminous yellow and ivory bands. Sovereign of all feathered creatures and emblem of the Empress and virtuous rule, the fenghuang's five-colored plumage traditionally encoded the five Confucian cardinal virtues.

title: Polychrome Glazed-Tile Dragons of the Datong Nine-Dragon Wall
medium: High-relief polychrome glazed architectural terracotta tiles (liuli)
creator: Shanxi imperial liuli tilemasters
repository: In situ, Former Palace of Zhu Gui (Prince of Dai), Datong
anatomy: coiling ochre and cobalt-glazed scaled bodies
pursuit of the flaming pearl amid waves
description: Erected in 1392 to screen the palace gate of Zhu Gui, thirteenth son of the Ming founder Hongwu, the 45.5-meter Datong screen is the oldest and largest extant Nine-Dragon Wall in China. Molded in bold polychrome liuli glazed tiles, its writhing dragons sport four claws—adhering strictly to Ming sumptuary law reserving five-clawed dragons for the Emperor alone—as they chase flaming pearls over foaming seas.

title: Gilt-Bronze Sculpture of Xuanwu (Black Tortoise and Snake)
medium: Cast copper alloy with mercury gilding
creator: Imperial Ming court foundry (commissioned for Mount Wudang)
description: Cast and richly gilded by imperial workshops during the Yongle Emperor's massive reconstruction of the Daoist temples on Mount Wudang, this sculpture depicts Xuanwu—the Dark Warrior of the Northern Quadrant—in its primordial zoomorphic form as a tortoise locked in sinuous embrace with a serpent. Revered as both a celestial directional guardian and the martial deity Zhenwu, the dual creature symbolized longevity, water, and cosmic yin-yang union.

title: Auspicious Qilin Tribute from Bengal (Ruiying Qilin Tu)
medium: Ink and color on silk hanging scroll
creator: Shen Du (沈度, 1357–1434, calligrapher) and Ming court painter
anatomy: reticulated coat likened to luminous scales
description: When envoys from Bengal—sailing in the wake of Admiral Zheng He's Indian Ocean Treasure Fleets—presented an East African giraffe to the Yongle court in September 1414, courtiers hailed the exotic creature—called girin in Somali—as a living manifestation of the mythical qilin. Inscribed above by Hanlin calligrapher Shen Du with a celebratory paean, the scroll exemplifies how Imperial Chinese statecraft assimilated natural marvels into classical omen-mythology.

title: River God Bingyi (Hebo) Riding Twin Dragons (Shan Hai Jing)
medium: Woodblock print, ink on paper
creator: Jiang Yinghao (蔣應鎬, illustrator)
repository: Rare Book Editions of the 1597 Illustrated Shan Hai Jing
anatomy: anthropomorphic river spirit astride twin dragons
description: Engraved for the landmark 1597 Wanli woodblock edition of the Classic of Mountains and Seas (Shan Hai Jing), Plate LXI depicts Bingyi—the abyssal lord of the Yellow River depths—gliding across turbulent waters astride a pair of harnessed horned dragons. According to the 'Guideways Within the Seas: North,' Bingyi dwells beneath the icy abysses (yuan) and commands the flood-dragons of China's inland seas.

title: The Headless Warrior Xingtian (Shan Hai Jing)
medium: Woodblock print, ink on paper
creator: Jiang Yinghao (蔣應鎬, illustrator)
repository: Illustrated Classic of Mountains and Seas (Haiwai Xijing)
anatomy: twin eyes formed from chest nipples
grinning mouth formed at the navel
description: Illustrating the 'Classic of Regions Beyond the Seas: West' in the Shan Hai Jing, Jiang Yinghao's late Ming woodcut portrays Xingtian after the Supreme Deity severed his head in cosmic battle and buried it beneath Mount Changyang. Refusing defeat, the indomitable giant transformed his nipples into staring eyes and his navel into a roaring mouth, dancing eternally with battle-axe and shield.

title: The Nine-Tailed Fox of Mount Qingqiu (Shan Hai Jing)
medium: Woodblock print, ink on mulberry paper
creator: Jiang Yinghao (蔣應鎬, illustrator) & Li Wenxiao (李文孝, engraver)
repository: Harvard-Yenching Library (Chongzhen Edition of Shan Hai Jing)
anatomy: fan of nine bushy fox tails
pointed vulpine snout and pricked ears
description: Cut by engraver Li Wenxiao after drawings by Jiang Yinghao for the Chongzhen-era Shan Hai Jing, this folio from the 'Classic of the Southern Mountains' depicts the nine-tailed fox of Mount Qingqiu, whose cry sounds like a human infant. Ambivalent in early Chinese lore—both a man-devouring mountain beast whose flesh wards off gu-poison and an auspicious marital omen before later becoming a shapeshifting trickster—the jiuweihu inspired fox traditions across East Asia.

title: The Winged Rain-Dragon Yinglong (Shan Hai Jing)
medium: Woodblock print, ink on paper
creator: Unknown Ming-Qing woodblock illustrator
repository: Early Modern Woodblock Edition of the Shan Hai Jing
anatomy: broad feathered wings sprouting from the shoulders
description: Unlike standard Chinese dragons that soar effortlessly through clouds without wings, Yinglong ('Responsive Dragon') is distinguished in classical woodblock editions of the Shan Hai Jing by a pair of sweeping feathered wings. Celebrated in myth as the martial rain-dragon who slew the rebels Chiyou and Kuafu for the Yellow Emperor and later carved river channels across China with his tail for Yu the Great, Yinglong commands both stormwaters and deluge.

title: Imperial Bronze Qilin of the Summer Palace
localName: 頤和園仁壽殿銅麒麟 (Tóng Qílín)
originLocation: Originally Yuanmingyuan; relocated to the Hall of Benevolence and Longevity, Summer Palace, Beijing
medium: Cast bronze
creator: Qing Imperial Household Department (Zaobanchu) foundry
anatomy: overlapping carp scales covering the body
bushy curled lion tail and flame-wisps
description: Cast with the imperial reign mark of the Qianlong Emperor on its crown and originally stationed at the Old Summer Palace (Yuanmingyuan) before its 1937 transfer to Yiheyuan, this monumental bronze qilin displays the canonical late-imperial composite anatomy: a dragon's head, deer's antlers, fish-scaled body, ox's hooves, and lion's tail. Standing before the Hall of Benevolence and Longevity, it embodied sagely governance and judicial discernment.

title: Imperial Bronze Guardian Lions (Shishi) of the Forbidden City
medium: Cast and gilded bronze on carved marble pedestals
creator: Qing Imperial Palace Foundry
repository: In situ, Forbidden City (Palace Museum), Beijing
anatomy: rows of tight snail-shell mane curls (luofa)
paw resting on embroidered cosmic sphere or cub
stylized roaring jaws and bulging eyes
description: Flanking the ceremonial thresholds of the Forbidden City in yin-yang pairs, these Qing bronze guardian lions transform the Asiatic lion—originally introduced via Buddhist Silk Road art—into a thoroughly mythologized imperial protector. Crowned with auspicious rows of tight curls reserved for the highest palatial rank, the male lion secures a latticework cosmic sphere beneath his right paw to signify universal sovereignty, while the female nurtures a cub beneath her left.

title: Imperial Ceremonial Headdress (Dianzi) with Pearl-Studded Fenghuang
medium: Gilt silver wire, kingfisher feathers (diancui), freshwater pearls, tourmaline, rubies, and jadeite
creator: Qing Imperial Palace Workshops (attributed to regalia of Empress Dowager Cixi)
anatomy: trembling spring-mounted beaks holding pearl drops
description: Associated with the court wardrobe of Empress Dowager Cixi, this sumptuous Manchu Qing dianzi headdress swarms with sculpted fenghuang phoenixes crafted from iridescent turquoise kingfisher feathers (diancui), gilt filigree, gemstones, and hundreds of luminous Manchurian pearls. Mounted on delicate wire springs that quivered with every movement of the wearer, the phoenixes proclaimed supreme female imperial authority.
